title: Grated Veggies, Blended Tofu: A 23-Gram Protein Savoury Pancake Recipe
excerpt: Fitness influencer Vanshika Khurana's savoury pancake folds shredded vegetables and blended tofu into a rice-flour batter — a 23-gram-protein recipe she shared on Instagram on September 8.
body:
• Fitness influencer Vanshika Khurana (Fit.Khurana) shared a savoury pancake she says delivers 23 grams of protein, built on 160 g of blended silken tofu and 35 g of rice flour.
  • A full cup of shredded zucchini, carrot, onion and cabbage goes into the batter, — fibre without a plate of raw vegetables.
  • Blend the tofu smooth, fold it into a seasoned rice-flour batter with the grated vegetables, cook thin and crisp in a lightly oiled pan, and serve with a soy-lemon dressing.
  • Hindustan Times reports the recipe from an Instagram video shared on September 8, and notes it has not independently verified the nutrition claims.

A savoury pancake built around 23 grams of protein

Fitness influencer Vanshika Khurana, who posts as Fit.Khurana, shared this savoury pancake — shredded vegetables folded into a tofu-and-rice-flour batter, cooked crisp and served with a soy-lemon dipping sauce — in an Instagram video on September 8. According to Hindustan Times, Khurana says she lost 40 kilos and reversed PCOS without giving up the food she enjoys.

Her pitch targets reluctant vegetable eaters: grate whatever sits in the fridge and bury it in batter. "If you eat just a single slice of tomato or a tiny bit of leafy greens and call it a 'veggie day,' listen up."

"When was the last time you ate two cups of veggies? Instead of letting vegetables rot in the fridge, make these 23 gram protein pancakes."

— Vanshika Khurana, fitness influencer (Fit.Khurana)

The fibre case for grating, not plating

Behind the recipe is a sound nutritional idea. Fibre supports more than gut health, Hindustan Times notes: it plays a role in digestion, blood sugar regulation and satiety, which can help with weight management. Grating vegetables into dishes people already like is the workaround.

For Indian households, the format feels instantly familiar: it is a vegetable-loaded cheela rebuilt with silken tofu and a soy-lemon dip. The classic moong dal cheela is already described as a protein-rich, high-fibre breakfast of roughly 180–200 kcal for two pieces, according to Balanced Bites.

What's inside: tofu for protein, rice flour for structure

The protein comes from one source: 160 g of silken tofu, blended smooth. The batter is rice flour with a spoonful of cornstarch, seasoned with salt, red chilli powder and black pepper. Shredded zucchini, carrot, onion and cabbage bring the fibre and bulk, black sesame seeds top each pancake, and the batch needs barely a teaspoon of oil.

One caveat: the 23-gram figure is Khurana's claim, and Hindustan Times states plainly that its article is based on unverified user-generated social media content. Treat the number as the creator's estimate, not a lab result.

"For protein, just blend paneer or tofu and add it in."

— Vanshika Khurana, fitness influencer (Fit.Khurana)

The full recipe

Ingredients:

  • 160 g silken tofu
  • 35 g rice flour
  • 1 tbsp cornstarch (about 8 g)
  • ¼ cup shredded zucchini
  • ½ carrot, shredded
  • ½ onion, finely sliced or shredded
  • ¼ cup shredded cabbage
  • Red chilli powder, to taste
  • Black pepper, to taste
  • Salt, to taste
  • 1 tsp black sesame seeds
  • 1 tsp oil, for cooking
  • Water, as required
  • Soy sauce, for serving

Method:

  1. Blend the silken tofu with a splash of water until completely smooth and creamy.
  2. In a large bowl, combine the rice flour and cornstarch. Add the shredded vegetables, season with salt, red chilli powder and black pepper, and mix well.
  3. Pour in the blended tofu and mix to a thick but pourable batter, adding a little water at a time if it feels too thick.
  4. Heat a lightly oiled non-stick pan over medium heat. Spoon small portions of batter on, spread each into a thin pancake, and sprinkle with black sesame seeds.
  5. Cook over medium-high until golden brown, crisp and set underneath, then flip and cook the other side. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding oil if needed.
  6. Serve hot with a soy sauce dressing made by mixing soy sauce, lemon juice, a little water, honey, salt and finely chopped green chilli.

The fine print, and why it still works

Two things hold the recipe together. Keep the batter thick but pourable and spread each pancake thin, or it will steam instead of crisp. And hold the 23-gram protein claim lightly — it is the creator's estimate, unverified by the publication that reported it. What remains is a practical template: protein-rich batter, a full cup of grated vegetables, minimal oil, and a dipping sauce with enough acid and heat to make it craveable.
